items.title: Tamil Nadu minister accuses DMK of AI-assisted corruption in library book purchases
items.summary: Tamil Nadu School Education Minister Rajmohan has accused the previous Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) government of procuring substandard books from dubious publishers for the Periyar Arivulagam library in Coimbatore. He alleged that the purchases involved the use of artificial intelligence and amounted to corruption. “For the first time in this country, the DMK has engaged in corruption using artificial intelligence,” Rajmohan said at a press conference in Chennai. Displaying a purchase order, the minister said the order for books from Agal Vilakku Publishers was issued on February 14, 2026, when the DMK was in power. The order specified that the books were to be delivered to the Periyar Arivulagam library, he said. Payments to the publishers were released in March 2026. Rajmohan alleged that the previous government had bought books that were fit to be thrown in a dustbin and had them delivered to the library before the Assembly elections in May 2026. He said the boxes were opened only after the elections, ahead of the library's inauguration, and pointed to a June 2026 seal on them as evidence of when they were opened. The minister also alleged that similar books had been procured for four other libraries that are yet to open: Kamarajar Arivulagam in Tiruchy, Bharathidasan Arivulagam in Salem, Anjalai Ammal Arivulagam in Cuddalore and Quide-e-Millath Arivulagam in Tirunelveli. He said Rs 50 crore had been allocated for each of these libraries. Explaining the procurement process, Rajmohan said a committee meeting to select books for Periyar Arivulagam was held in November and December 2025, followed by another meeting in January 2026. The recommendation committee had 137 members, of whom 112 attended the meeting, he said. The recommendations were subsequently sent to a high-level committee for approval, which he alleged was secured through pressure from the DMK. items.title: Protest, suspension, legal battle: What is happening at Kerala’s Sankaracharya University
items.summary: “We are the students of this campus. Not violent protesters,” said Aswanth VM, a Malayalam-language PhD scholar at the Sree Sankaracharya University of Sanskrit (SSUS) in Kalady, Ernakulam. Aswanth is one of three students on an indefinite hunger strike in front of the university. They are demanding the university’s permission to sit for their examinations and for the revocation of suspensions of 16 students. “We will continue our protest until the university agrees to our demand,” Aswanth added. The protest has since spilt over to another campus, the Maharajah’s College in Ernakulam, where SFI students questioned the Education Minister over the issue and were themselves suspended. When TNM visited the university on October 5, the three students, Aswanth, Archana and KV Abhijith – also members of the Students Federation of India (SFI), the student organisation of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) [CPI(M)] – were on the fifth day of their hunger strike. What began as a student protest under SFI on July 22 later escalated into a dispute that reached the Supreme Court of India, with the students seeking a favourable judgement to write their semester examinations. On November 3, the SC declined to entertain the plea and directed a single bench of the Kerala High Court to hear and resolve the matter expeditiously. The court noted that the university gave assurances to conduct special examinations if the students receive a favourable ruling, as reflected in the official record. A doctor checking the health condition of the students who are on a hunger strike What triggered the controversy at the University? The SSUS witnessed protests over infrastructure, academic administration and other students' concerns for years. “This is not a new protest. For years, we have been holding protests here, raising various demands. Whenever some of our demands remain unfulfilled, we raise those demands again and continue our protests. It was in that context that we resumed the protest on July 22," Rithisha, Kerala’s first transgender PhD student and one among the 16 suspended students, said. On July 22, the students raised an 18-point charter of demands concerning campus rights, infrastructure, and academic administration. The students also complained that the Vice Chancellor Ciza Thomas, was at the university on most days, and this was causing academic delays. The protest took another turn on August 13, during the first meeting of the university's reconstituted syndicate.
